actions.name: Occurs in at least one protected area
Subject to any international management / trade controls

documentation.range: This species is distributed from Djibouti and Somalia through much of East Africa (where it is widespread in Tanzania and Kenya, but is known from only the Amudat-Moroto area in Uganda and is not known to occur in Rwanda or Burundi - Spawls et al. 2002), to Botswana, Namibia, Mozambique and South Africa (Spawls et al. 2002, Largen and Spawls 2010, Ineich 2001). In Ethiopia and Kenya its distribution reaches the border with South Sudan, but it appears not to occur in this country or in Sudan (Phillips 2004). Bayless (2002) report an isolated specimen-based record far north of the main distribution in Bahig, in the Matruh District of northern Egypt. In South Africa it is absent from the western parts of the Western Cape and the central and western portions of the Northern Cape, although there is some evidence of recent range extension in the Northern Cape (Alexander and Marais 2007). It is also largely absent from Highveld Grassland in the central parts of South Africa. Some records from Lesotho (Ambrose 2006) and Eastern Cape (Visser 1984) require confirmation. It ranges from sea level to around 2,000 m asl (Spawls et al. 2002, Largen and Spawls 2010).
documentation.population: This species can be abundant in some areas, particularly where refuge sites exist (Spawls et al. 2002). It is rare in Djibouti (Ineich 2001), close to the northern limit of its range. It is widespread and abundant in South Africa (Alexander and Marais 2007).
documentation.habitats: This diurnal and mostly terrestrial species inhabits dry and moist savanna, coastal thicket, woodland and semi-desert (Spawls et al. 2002). It uses a variety of shelter sites, including rock fissures, hollow trees, abandoned termite hills, mammal burrows and abandoned beehives (Spawls et al. 2002). Clutches of 8 to 51 eggs are laid by the female (Spawls et al. 2002).
documentation.threats: There do not appear to be any major threats to this widespread monitor species. Although it is harvested to some degree exploitation is thought unlikely to threaten most species of monitor lizard, which tend to be abundant (Pernetta 2009 and refs therein). The white-throated monitor is not among the more heavily-traded species, comprising approximately 2% of the global documented trade in varanids between 1975 and 2005, and its range does not include any of the African countries considered major exporters of reptile species (Pernetta 2009).
documentation.measures: In view of its wide range the species is presumed to occur in a number of protected areas. An assessment of the impacts of harvesting for traditional medicine in South Africa may be beneficial. In the South African regional Red List assessment the species' conservation status is Least Concern.  The species is included in CITES Appendix II.
documentation.use_trade: This species is found in the international pet trade. It does not appear to be exploited for its skin. Between 1975 and 2005, CITES documented the export of 26,079 live White-throated Monitors from 14 countries (Pernetta 2009); although Varanus albigularis is not known from this many countries. Mozambique is one of the major exporting countries of wild specimens (CITES trade database). The skin and fat of this species is used in the 'muti' trade in South Africa (Alexander and Marais 2007).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Least Concern on the basis that, while any threats to this species are poorly-known, it is widespread and there is no evidence of substantial declines. Harvesting pressures on this species are thought to be low, and so it is probably not at immediate risk from international trade.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: The status of Varanus ocellatus is uncertain; it has been variously treated as a synonym of either V. albigularis or V. exanthematicus (Bennett 2004). This account follows Bennett (2004) in considering this form a synonym of V. exanthematicus with a distribution in Sudan (presumably South Sudan given the distribution for V. exanthematicus provided by this author). Specimens from Djibouti, Somalia and Ethiopia previously attributed to V. ocellatus are now understood to represent V. albigularis (Ineich 2001, Largen and Spawls 2006). A phylogeographic study comparing populations throughout the range of V. albigularis would be informative, including clarification of the status of forms previously recognized as subspecies but rejected by Broadley and Howell (1991), and the currently recognized subspecies V. a. angolensis. Currently three subspecies are recognized: Varanus a. albigularis (southern Africa, north to Angola, Zambia, Mozambique), V. albigularis angolensis (Angola, Namibia, Zambia, DR Congo), V. albigularis microstictus (northeastern Africa, Ethiopia to northern and central Mozambique) (Auliya and Koch 2020).
